knowledge-argument: The knowledge argument, framed by Frank Jackson through the thought experiment of Mary the color scientist, challenges physicalism about the mind. Mary knows every physical fact about color vision while confined to a black-and-white room; the argument contends that when she finally sees red she learns something new—what the experience is actually like. If she gains new knowledge, the reasoning goes, then not all facts are physical facts, and subjective conscious experience (qualia) escapes a purely physical description. Physicalists have replied that Mary gains a new ability or mode of acquaintance rather than a new fact.
what-is-it-like: In his 1974 essay "What Is It Like to Be a Bat?", Thomas Nagel argues that consciousness has an irreducibly subjective character: for any conscious creature there is something it is like to be that creature, experienced from its own point of view. Because a bat perceives the world through echolocation, we cannot genuinely imagine its inner life from the inside, only picture what it would be like for us to behave as a bat does. Nagel uses this to press a limit on objective, physical accounts of the mind, which describe things from no particular perspective and so seem to leave out the very feature—subjective experience—that makes a state conscious.
parfit-teleportation: The teleporter and fission cases, developed by Derek Parfit, test what personal identity really consists in. If a machine scans and destroys you, then builds an exact replica elsewhere, is the replica you or merely a copy—and does the answer change if the original is not destroyed, or if two replicas are made? Parfit argues that in such fission scenarios there is no determinate fact about which future person is you, and concludes that identity is not what matters for survival. What matters instead is psychological continuity and connectedness, and recognizing this, he suggests, should loosen our fixation on the persistence of a single self.
a-series-time: J.M.E. McTaggart distinguished two ways of ordering events in time. The A-series ranks them as past, present, or future—positions that continually shift as what was future becomes present and then past—while the B-series orders them by the fixed relations of earlier-than and later-than. McTaggart argued that the A-series is essential to real change yet incoherent, since any event must possess all three incompatible properties of pastness, presentness, and futurity, and he concluded that time itself is unreal. The distinction has framed modern debate between tensed theories of time, which take the passage of the present seriously, and tenseless theories built on the B-series.
free-will-determinism: The free will problem asks whether human beings can act freely and be morally responsible if every event, including our choices, is fixed by prior causes. Determinism holds that the state of the world at any moment, together with the laws of nature, necessitates exactly one future, which seems to leave no room for genuine alternatives. Hard determinists conclude that free will is therefore an illusion, while libertarians insist that we do possess a freedom incompatible with determinism and so deny that determinism is true of our choices. The dispute bears directly on praise, blame, punishment, and desert.
compatibilism: Compatibilism is the view that free will and determinism can both be true: even if our actions are causally determined, we can still act freely in the sense that matters for moral responsibility. On this account, an action is free when it flows from the agent's own desires and reasoning without external coercion or compulsion, regardless of whether those states were themselves caused. Associated with thinkers from Hobbes and Hume to contemporary philosophers like Harry Frankfurt, compatibilism reframes freedom as a matter of the right kind of control rather than an ability to have done otherwise under identical conditions. Critics charge that this redefines freedom rather than securing the deeper autonomy people intuitively want.
personal-identity: Personal identity concerns what makes someone the same person over time despite change, and what the self fundamentally is. Philosophers have offered competing criteria: the body or brain, continuity of memory and psychology, or the persistence of an immaterial soul. Locke's memory-based view, Hume's bundle theory that finds no enduring self behind experiences, and later refinements have all sought to say why the child and the adult, or the person before and after profound change, count as one and the same. The question matters for responsibility, anticipation, survival, and the concern we have for our own futures.
simulation-hypothesis: The simulation hypothesis proposes that our reality might be a computer simulation run by an advanced civilization rather than a base physical world. In a 2003 argument, Nick Bostrom contended that at least one of three claims must hold: civilizations almost always go extinct before reaching the capacity to run such simulations, advanced civilizations rarely choose to run many ancestor simulations, or we are very probably living in one. The reasoning turns on the thought that if sophisticated simulations became feasible and common, simulated minds would vastly outnumber original ones. The hypothesis revives ancient skeptical worries about appearance and reality in a technological form.
time-travel: The metaphysics of time travel examines whether travel to the past or future is coherent and what constraints it would impose. The chief puzzle is the grandfather paradox: if you could go back and prevent your own existence, you would undo the very journey that made this possible, so something must stop you. Philosophers such as David Lewis argue that time travel need not be contradictory, provided the past is fixed and the traveler's actions were always already part of it, ruling out any change to what has happened. Related debates concern causal loops, personal versus external time, and which theories of time even permit backward travel.
bergson-duration: Duration (durée) is Henri Bergson's name for time as it is actually lived and felt, as opposed to time as measured by clocks. Real duration is a continuous, qualitative flow in which past and present interpenetrate and each moment is genuinely new, unlike the homogeneous, divisible instants that science treats as spatial units laid side by side. Bergson argued that intellect and physics distort time by spatializing it, and that only intuition grasps duration from within. The idea grounds his views on memory, freedom, and creativity, and shaped much of early twentieth-century thought.
bergson-elan-vital: Élan vital is the vital impetus that Henri Bergson placed at the heart of his 1907 work Creative Evolution. Against mechanistic and strictly Darwinian accounts, which he saw as explaining life only by external causes, Bergson proposed a creative, forward-pushing life force that drives evolution toward novel and unpredictable forms. Life, on this view, is not the unfolding of a preset plan but an ongoing creative surge that continually invents new solutions and diverges into branching lineages. Though influential in its day and admired by many artists and writers, the notion drew criticism for its vagueness and lack of empirical grounding.
bergson-memory: In Matter and Memory (1896), Henri Bergson set out to clarify the relation between mind and body by rethinking perception and recollection. He distinguished habit-memory, the bodily repetition of learned actions, from pure or spontaneous memory, which conserves the past in its entirety and is not stored in the brain like a thing. On his account the brain is an organ of action that filters and channels memory toward present needs rather than a warehouse of images, so mind and matter differ in degree and rhythm rather than being wholly separate substances. The book advanced Bergson's larger claim that consciousness is fundamentally temporal, gathering the past into the living present.
bergson-laughter: In his 1900 essay Laughter, Henri Bergson analyzed the comic as arising when we perceive "something mechanical encrusted upon the living." We laugh, he argued, at rigidity, repetition, and automatism in what ought to be supple and adaptive—a person behaving like a machine, a stiff gesture, an absent-minded slip into routine. Laughter thus serves a social function, gently correcting the inelastic and demanding that people stay flexibly attentive to life. The account ties his theory of comedy to his broader philosophy of duration, spontaneity, and the difference between the living and the merely mechanical.
freud-unconscious: The unconscious is the cornerstone of Sigmund Freud's psychoanalysis: a region of the mind holding thoughts, memories, and desires that are hidden from awareness yet powerfully shape feeling and behavior. Freud held that many such contents are actively repressed because they are threatening or unacceptable, and that they resurface in disguised form through dreams, slips of the tongue, symptoms, and jokes. Interpreting these expressions was, for him, the route to understanding neurosis and the self. The claim that we are not transparent to ourselves—that much mental life is inaccessible to introspection—has been enormously influential and much contested.
freud-death-drive: The death drive, sometimes called Thanatos, is the concept Sigmund Freud introduced in Beyond the Pleasure Principle (1920) to name a fundamental urge toward dissolution, aggression, and a return to an inanimate state. He proposed it to explain phenomena the pleasure principle could not, such as the compulsion to repeat traumatic experiences and the persistence of self-destructive behavior. Set against Eros, the life drive that binds and preserves, the death drive expresses a countervailing tendency toward discharge, destruction, and the undoing of tension. The idea remains among Freud's most speculative and disputed, yet influential in later psychoanalytic and cultural theory.
